steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A pictogram uses symbols or pictures to represent data; each symbol represents a fixed quantity stated in the key.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: In a pie chart, the angle of each sector is proportional to the frequency it represents: angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: To construct a pie chart, calculate each sector angle, draw a circle, and use a protractor to measure each angle from the previous sector.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A stem-and-leaf diagram displays data in order while retaining the original values; the stem shows the leading digits and the leaf shows the final digit.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: In a pie chart, a category has frequency 15 out of a total of 60. What angle should its sector have? | Q: A stem-and-leaf diagram has stem 4 and leaves 2, 5, 7, 8. What are the actual data values if the key is 4 | 2 means 42? | Q: In a Venn diagram, set A has 20 elements, set B has 15 elements, and A ∩ B has 8 elements. How many elements are in A ∪ B?

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always include a key on stem-and-leaf diagrams and pictograms — you will lose marks without one. When drawing pie charts, always label each sector with the category name and preferably the percentage or frequency. In a Venn diagram, the region outside both circles represents elements that are in neither set — do not forget this in probability questions. When comparing two datasets using a back-to-back stem-and-leaf, comment on the shape, median, and spread. Population pyramids can show ageing populations (narrow base, wide top) or young populations (wide base, narrow top) — use these terms in your comparisons.
